newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINLAND NOT KEEN TO UP RATES, REVALUE FIM-DEUTSCHE.
newsitem.headline: FINLAND NOT KEEN TO UP RATES, REVALUE FIM-DEUTSCHE.

text.p: The Bank of Finland will be reluctant to hike interest rates and so add pressure on the markka to strengthen further against the mark, investment Bank Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said in a research note dated July 28.
The appreciation of the markka would be moderated as the markets begin to price in rising German interest rates, it said.

"We believe that the central bank will be reluctant to hike interest rates to any large extent as this would only put further pressure on the FIM, which is already trading above its ERM central rate," it said. The markka's central parity to the German mark in Europe's exchange rate mechanism is 3.04.
The appreciation of the markka, underway since early June, had "fuelled speculation that the FIM will have to be revalued ahead of the final fixing of exchange rates for EMU," Deutsche said.
It referred to the markka's advance to 2.94 per mark -- more than three percent above the ERM midpoint.

"While further upward pressure on the FIM/DEM exchange rate is possible as the market looks for an early hike in interest rates given the strength of the Finnish economy and the risks of higher inflation, we believe that Finland will be reluctant to revalue its currency," it said.

Forecasting the mark-dollar exchange rate to trade in a 1.80-1.85 range for the rest of the year, Deutsche said "...and eventually the market will begin to price in rising German interest rates as growth accelerates. This is expected to have a moderating effect on FIM appreciation."

The bank said its Natural Real Exchange Rates currency valuation model suggested that the markka was not "substantially undervalued" and that its equilibrium value against the mark was 3.00 at the end of Q1, 1997.
Deutsche said its model implied that the current phase of strength did not warrant a revaluation of the markka.

"In addition the central bank will be reluctant to revalue the FIM given that Sweden will remain outside EMU in 1999 and would therefore retain the option of devaluing the SEK," it said, adding this could pose a problem for Finnish forestry firms, whose main European competitors are Swedish companies.

"The central bank therefore faces a dilemma in that it presumably wants to hike interest rates given the strength of the economy, but is reluctant to do so as it would put further pressure on the FIM," Deutsche said.
Any tightening -- in case of rising inflation or excessive 1998 pay rises -- would be "only moderate, say 25 bp," it said.
